unit.title: Comply with organizational requirements for protection and use of intellectual property

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What two-word term names a creator's right to be named as the author of a work, which may stay with the creator even after the copyright is sold?
What one-word term names the permission an IP owner gives another party to use the IP on set terms?
What two-letter mark is placed beside a brand name to claim it as a trade mark before it is registered?
A program is needed by 35 staff. Each licence covers 5 users. How many licences must the organisation buy?
What one-word term names giving credit to the creator and source when you use their work?
What one-word term names passing off someone else's written work or ideas as your own?
What two-word term describes software whose source code is published under a licence that lets others use and change it?
What two-word term names the status of a work whose copyright has expired, so that anyone may use it?

What word does the symbol © stand for?

A firm's trade mark was registered in 2019. Its registration lasts 10 years before it must be renewed. In which year is the renewal due?
What one-word term names a planned check of an organisation's computers to confirm that every program is properly licensed?
What two-word term names the rule that staff must put papers away and leave their desks clear when they are not there?
A design team created 64 designs this year. The IP procedure requires each one to be logged, and 48 have been logged. What percentage has been logged?

essays.stem: Explain the main parts an organisational intellectual property policy should contain, and how a supervisor can make sure her team follows it.
essays.modelAnswer: An IP policy should state its purpose and who it covers, including staff, contractors and volunteers. It should explain the kinds of IP the organisation owns and uses, such as trade marks, copyright, designs, inventions and confidential information. It should say that work created by staff in their jobs belongs to the organisation, and how new IP must be recorded and reported. It should set rules for using other people's material: check the licence, get written permission, credit the source and keep records. It should cover software licences, confidentiality marking, social media and what happens when staff leave. It should name the IP officer, explain how to report a breach and state the consequences of breaking the rules. A supervisor makes it work by briefing the team, giving each person a short summary and the full policy, and building checks into normal work, such as a permission check before anything is published. She should spot-check work and licence records, answer questions or pass them to the IP officer, correct problems quickly and fairly, and suggest updates when the policy no longer fits how the team works.
markingPoints: Scope and the types of IP covered
Ownership of staff work and how new IP is recorded and reported
Rules for using others' IP, software and confidential information
Named contact, breach reporting and consequences
Supervisor briefs the team, builds in checks, spot-checks and raises updates

essays.stem: Staff at a Kingston advertising agency often use images, music, fonts and video clips from the internet in client work. Describe the procedure you would put in place so that they use other people's IP lawfully.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would make the rule clear: material found online belongs to someone, and it may be used only if the agency holds a licence or written permission. I would set up approved sources, such as paid stock libraries and music services with business licences, and keep the licence terms on a shared drive. Before using any item, the designer would check that the licence covers the use, for example print, broadcast, social media or resale, and the territory and time period. For anything outside the approved sources, the designer would ask the owner for written permission and send it to the studio manager. Each job would have a simple rights log listing every third-party item, its source, licence or permission, any credit required and the expiry date. The account manager would check the log before work goes to the client, and the client would be told of any limits on use. Fonts and software would be bought for business use only. Staff would be trained at induction, and the log would be spot-checked each month, with problems corrected before they reach the public.
markingPoints: Rule that online material needs a licence or permission
Approved licensed sources and checking the scope of each licence
Written permission for other items, kept on file
Rights log per job checked before release
Training and regular spot checks

essays.stem: Explain an employee's responsibilities for protecting the organisation's IP and confidential information, from joining the organisation to leaving it.
essays.modelAnswer: On joining, the employee reads and signs the employment contract, including its IP and confidentiality terms, and attends induction on the IP policy. She declares any IP she owned before joining, so it is recorded as hers and not confused with the organisation's. She must not bring in confidential material from a former employer. While working, she treats designs, plans, prices, client lists and other marked information as confidential, keeps it locked away or password protected and shares it only with people who are authorised. She records and reports new work, such as designs or improvements, to the IP officer quickly and does not disclose it outside before protection is in place. She uses only licensed software and checks permissions before using others' material. She reports any misuse she sees, inside or outside the organisation. On leaving, she returns all documents, files and devices, does not keep copies, has her access closed and is reminded that her duty of confidentiality continues. Each of these steps protects the organisation's value and its legal position.
markingPoints: Signs IP and confidentiality terms and attends induction
Declares prior IP and brings in no confidential material from old employers
Protects confidential information and uses licensed material only
Records and reports new IP and any misuse
Returns all material on leaving, with continuing confidentiality

essays.stem: A routine check at a public agency in Spanish Town shows 18 more copies of a design program installed than the licences held. Describe the steps you would take, and how you would stop it happening again.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first confirm the finding by checking the installation list against the licence records, to be sure of the exact number and the computers involved. I would report it at once to my manager and the officer responsible for IT and IP, because the agency is using software it has not paid for. Next, I would find out which staff actually need the program. Copies that are not needed would be removed and the removal recorded. For the users who do need it, I would get a quotation for 18 more licences, or fewer if some copies are removed, and seek approval to buy them under the agency's procurement rules. I would find out how the extra copies were installed, for example through shared installation files or staff with administrator rights. To stop it happening again, only the IT unit should be able to install software, every request should be approved and logged, and the licence register should be checked against installed copies at least every quarter. Staff would be reminded of the policy and the reasons for it.
markingPoints: Confirms the facts against licence records
Reports to the right officers promptly
Removes unneeded copies and buys licences through proper procurement
Finds the cause of the extra installs
Controls installs, keeps the register and checks it regularly

essays.stem: Explain why staff should record and report the new IP they create at work, and describe a suitable reporting procedure.
essays.modelAnswer: New products, designs, processes, software and written materials can be valuable to an organisation, but it can protect and use them only if it knows they exist. Some protection, such as a patent or registered design, may be lost if the idea is shown in public before an application is filed. Records with dates and names also prove who created the work and when, which helps if ownership is ever disputed. A suitable procedure would ask staff to keep dated drafts and working notes in the shared work system, not on personal devices. When something new is created, the staff member completes a short disclosure form describing it, who created it, the date and whether anyone outside has seen it. The form goes to the supervisor and then the IP officer within an agreed time, such as five working days. The IP officer decides whether to register it, keep it confidential or simply record it, and enters it in the IP register. The staff member is told the outcome and thanked, and is reminded not to discuss it outside until a decision is made.
markingPoints: Organisation can only protect what it knows about
Early disclosure can destroy some protection
Dated records prove creation and ownership
Clear steps: disclosure form, supervisor, IP officer, time limit
Decision recorded in the register and feedback to the creator

essays.stem: A staff member tells you that a former employee is using your firm's client training materials in his new business. Describe how you would handle the report in line with organisational requirements.
essays.modelAnswer: I would thank the staff member, listen carefully and write down what she has seen, when and where, and how she knows. I would ask her for any evidence she already has, such as a brochure, a web page or a recording, but tell her not to contact the former employee or post anything about it. I would keep the matter confidential and report it promptly to the IP officer or the person named in the IP policy, using the reporting form if there is one. I would help to collect further facts: the materials concerned, when they were created, who created them, and whether they carry the firm's copyright notice. I would check the former employee's contract for IP and confidentiality terms and whether he returned all materials when he left. I would not accuse him or take action myself, because the firm needs legal advice before it responds, and a hasty step could weaken its position or be unfair. Finally, I would record what was done and look at how materials could be better controlled in future.
markingPoints: Records the facts and gathers evidence without confronting anyone
Keeps it confidential and reports promptly through the policy
Checks ownership records and the former employee's contract terms
Leaves action to those authorised, after legal advice
Records the case and reviews controls

essays.stem: Evaluate the risks to an organisation's IP when staff post about their work on social media, and recommend rules to manage those risks.
essays.modelAnswer: Staff posts can help an organisation by showing its work and culture, but they carry real IP risks. A photo of a prototype or a new design posted early may destroy the chance to protect it and gives rivals a head start. Posts can reveal confidential information, such as client names, prices or plans, often in the background of a photo. Staff may use music, images or brand logos that belong to others, which can lead to claims against the organisation. They may also misuse the organisation's own logo in ways that harm its image. I recommend a short social media rule within the IP policy. Staff should not post anything about unreleased products, designs or client work without approval. Only the communications team should use the organisation's logo and official accounts. Staff should check photos for confidential material in the background before posting work-related images. They should use only content they own or have permission to use, and should not claim to speak for the organisation. Staff should be trained on these rules, and concerns should be reported to the IP officer.
markingPoints: Recognises benefits as well as risks
Early disclosure and leaks of confidential information
Infringing others' IP and misuse of the organisation's brand
Clear approval and logo rules
Training and a route for reporting concerns

essays.stem: Plan a one-hour induction session on intellectual property for new staff joining a hotel group in Montego Bay.
essays.modelAnswer: Aim: new staff will know what IP the hotel group owns and uses, and what the policy requires of them. In the first ten minutes I would explain what IP is, using hotel examples: the group's name and logo, menus, photos, its website and booking system, guest data and recipes. In the next fifteen minutes I would cover their own duties: work they create belongs to the group, confidential information such as rates and guest details must be protected, and new ideas should be reported. Then, for fifteen minutes, I would cover using others' IP: music in public areas needs a licence, which the group holds, so staff must not play their own playlists; photos, videos and logos need permission; and only licensed software may be installed. In ten minutes I would use short scenarios in pairs, such as a guest asking for a copy of a recipe or a friend asking for rates. In the final ten minutes I would explain how to report concerns, give out the policy summary and a contact card, and use a short quiz to check understanding. Attendance would be recorded.
markingPoints: Clear aim and timed plan
Hotel examples of IP owned and used
Staff duties on ownership, confidentiality and reporting
Using others' IP correctly, including music and software
Active methods, check of understanding and record of attendance

essays.stem: Explain how an organisation should manage contractors and suppliers so that its own IP, and the IP of others, is respected.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work starts, the organisation should use a written contract, not a verbal agreement. The contract should say who will own the IP in anything the contractor creates, such as designs, software or reports, and, where the organisation is to own it, include an assignment to the organisation on payment. It should include a confidentiality clause, or a separate non-disclosure agreement, covering all information shared. The contractor should promise that the work is original or properly licensed and that it does not infringe anyone else's rights, so that the organisation is not exposed to claims. The organisation should share only what the contractor needs, marked confidential, and limit system access. During the work, the manager should check that third-party material, such as stock images or code libraries, is licensed for the organisation's use, and collect the licence details. At the end, the contractor should hand over all source files and records, return or destroy confidential material and lose access. The new IP should be recorded in the IP register. These steps protect the organisation's ownership and avoid infringing others' rights.
markingPoints: Written contract stating ownership and assignment of new IP
Confidentiality clause or NDA and limited sharing
Promise of originality and licensed third-party material
Checks during the work and handover of files at the end
Recording the new IP and ending access

essays.stem: Justify why an organisation should respect the intellectual property of others, giving legal, financial and reputational reasons.
essays.modelAnswer: Respecting others' IP is first a legal duty. Intellectual property law gives owners rights to control copying and use of their work, brands, designs and inventions. If an organisation copies software, music, images or logos without permission, the owner can take legal action, ask a court to stop the use and claim damages. The financial reasons follow from this. An organisation may have to pay damages and legal costs, buy licences at full price after the event, withdraw and reprint materials, or stop selling a product. These costs are usually far higher than the cost of licensing correctly at the start. The reputational reasons are just as important. Clients, partners and the public expect an organisation to act honestly. News that a firm or public body used pirated software or copied another's design can damage trust, lose contracts and make it harder to defend its own IP, because it cannot credibly demand respect it does not give. Respecting others' IP also supports the creative and business community in Jamaica that the organisation depends on. For these reasons, compliance is a sound business decision.
markingPoints: Legal: owners can stop use and claim damages
Financial: damages, costs, reprinting and lost sales exceed licence costs
Reputational: trust, contracts and credibility in defending its own IP
Ethical and community reasons
Reaches a justified conclusion

practical1.title: Check a marketing pack and software records against the IP policy
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up organisation (for example a Kingston tour operator or a parish-based training institute). It contains a short IP policy, a draft brochure and slide presentation that use images, music, fonts, quotes and other firms' logos, a list of installed software, the licence records and a few permission emails. Some items comply and some do not. As a group, check every item against the policy and produce: a compliance checklist on screen or on paper listing each item, its owner, the licence or permission found, and whether it complies; a findings log of each problem, why it breaks the policy and the corrective action; and a one-page memo to the manager summarising the results and recommending actions, with owners and dates. Give each member a named role: team lead (plans the work, keeps time and writes the memo), materials checker for images and fonts, materials checker for music, video and quotes, software and licence checker, and records officer (builds the checklist and findings log). In a group of four, the team lead also builds the findings log. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Case pack from the assessor, including the IP policy, draft materials and licence records
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
Highlighters, sticky notes and a flipchart
photos: The group's plan on the flipchart, showing who checks which items
The draft brochure and slides marked up with the items checked
The compliance checklist on screen, with each item's result
The software count compared with the licence records
The findings log with corrective actions
The finished memo to the manager
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Checked each item against the policy, not against personal opinion
Identified the missing licences, permissions and credits in the pack
Worked out the software shortfall correctly from the records
Proposed practical corrective actions with owners and dates
Explained their findings clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up case material and do not copy real firms' logos
Keep the case pack and findings confidential to the group and the assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Write a staff IP procedure and deliver an induction briefing
practical2.brief: Your group has been asked by the manager of a made-up organisation (for example a Montego Bay hotel group or a public agency in Spanish Town) to help new staff follow the IP policy. Produce: a two-page staff procedure that covers using other people's material, protecting confidential information, recording and reporting new IP, and reporting suspected breaches; a one-page flowchart of the reporting steps; and a ten-minute induction briefing with no more than eight slides and a five-question quiz. Then deliver the briefing to the assessor and another group, who act as new staff and ask questions. Give each member a named role: lead writer (drafts the procedure and keeps time), flowchart designer, slide designer, quiz and scenario writer, and presenter (opens and closes the briefing; every member presents at least one slide). In a group of four, the lead writer also writes the quiz. Collect the quiz answers and record the questions asked. Photograph each stage.
materials: Short organisational IP policy from the assessor
Computers with word-processing and presentation software, and a projector or large screen
photos: The group's outline of the procedure on the flipchart
The group delivering the briefing, showing each presenter
The completed quiz sheets and the list of questions asked
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Procedure is accurate, clear and matches the policy
Flowchart shows who to report to and in what order
Presented their part clearly, using plain language
Answered questions correctly or said they would refer them to the IP officer
Quiz checks the key points of the procedure
Treated the audience and teammates with respect
safety: Use made-up names and examples only, not real people or real firms' material
Keep any personal quiz results confidential
Speak respectfully and let every member contribute
Keep cables tidy and the presentation area clear
